metadata.title: Two ontology design patterns in the domain of collections
metadata.venue: Web Semantics: Science, Services and Agents on the World Wide Web
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper presents two ontology design patterns, Permutation and ListOfPermutations, for representing collections of ordered elements without repetition. These patterns address recurring modeling problems in information management and provide a solution for effective modeling of collections.

sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
sections.text: Collections are objects used to arrange, into a single unit, multiple data items that form a natural group. Different types of collections exist, due to different constraints based on whether or not they impose an order on their elements and whether or not they allow repetition of elements. Any of them are easily found in several domains of our everyday life. For instance, a deck of cards, the prime divisors of a number or the teams that compete in a championship can be seen as a collection. Thus, an effective modeling of collections is a recurring issue in information management. In the ontology design field, recurring modeling problems can be addressed by the use of Ontology Design Patterns (ODPs). In the case of collections, ODPs have been proposed for representing sequences, lists, sets and bags. However, none of these patterns are completely adequate for representing collections of ordered elements without repetition. In this paper we present an ODP for representing that notion, which we have named Permutation . Moreover, another ODP named ListOfPermutations is also introduced, which allows to represent how the order of a Permutation varies along time. Because not all constraints required by these ODPs can be represented in OWL 2, SHACL shapes have been used in their definitions. 1.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The need to model the variation in the order of a set of elements over time may occur in many settings. For instance, in a sports league season, it could be interesting to collect how the ranking of the teams competing in the league varies along the season. Another scenario is that of the Alternating Treatments Design [ 1 ], a research methodology in which two o more treatments are alternated for several times, in blocks that contain all the different treatments in randomized order. These two scenarios, as well as others encountered in the real world, pose a similar modeling problem: the representation of lists of permu- tations of the same group of non-repeatable elements. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that their modeling solutions will also be alike. This brings us to the idea of design patterns. Design patterns arise from the need of avoiding repetitive search of solutions to modeling problems that have been previously solved in a proper manner. The idea was first introduced in 1977 in [ 2 ], where authors identified recurring problems in the fields of architecture and civil engineering, and it rapidly spread to other fields. One of the best known examples in the field of Computer Science is that of software design patterns for Software Engineering [ 3 ], but design patterns can also be found in other areas such as Human–Computer Interaction [ 4 ] or Cloud Computing [ 5 ]. ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail addresses: idoia.berges@ehu.eus (I. Berges), a.illarramendi@ehu.eus (A. Illarramendi). In the field of the Semantic Web, patterns are called Ontology Design Patterns (ODPs). ODPs are small ontologies that offer a con- ceptual design solution to certain use cases and should ideally meet, among others, the following requirements [ 6 ]: Be extendable but self- contained, minimize ontological constraints to foster reuse, address one or more explicit requirements (competency questions), be associatable to an ontology unit test, span more that one application area or domain, be the representation of a core notion in the domain of expertise, address a single invariant instead of targeting multiple recurring issues at the same time, be alignable to other patterns, and follow established modeling best practices. Although enabling reuse of domain knowledge was one of the driving forces in ontology research [ 7 ] and ontology reuse was pointed out as a promising approach for ontology engineering [ 8 ], some works in the related literature indicate that these recommendations are not a consolidated practice, neither in the case of ontologies [ 9 , 10 ], nor in the case of ODPs [ 11 ]. Thus, they highlight the need for developing tools and methods to facilitate reuse. In that sense, methodologies such as MOMo and its supporting tooling infrastructure CoModIDE have been proposed [ 12 ]. This methodology includes the systematic use of ODPs as one of its central aspects. The work also emphasizes the need of a curated ODP library, because although several ODPs have been published in portals such as ontologydesignpatterns.org , they vary in aspects such as documentation quality and completeness. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.websem.2025.100863 Received 20 September 2023; Received in revised form 10 January 2025; Accepted 28 January 2025 Journal of Web Semantics 85 (2025) 100863 2 I. Berges and A. Illarramendi In this paper we present two ODPs in the domain of collections: Permutation and ListOfPermutations . A collection is an object that allows to arrange multiple items that form a natural group into a single unit. They are widely used in information systems because they allow, among others, to store, search and manipulate data. Collections may involve groups of non-repeatable or repeatable items, and which may be ordered or unordered, giving rise to different types of collections. sections.heading: Background
sections.text: and related works There are some works in the specialized literature that address two relevant issues related to our work: the semantic representation of collections and the semantic representation of change over time. 2.1. Semantic representation of collections 2.1.1. The collections ontology The Collections Ontology 2 [ 14 ] is an ontology implemented in OWL 2 that allows the definition of three different kinds of collections: sets, bags and lists. One of the two top-level classes of the ontology is Collection , which can be considered as an abstract class that is then specialized by specific collection types. More precisely, a Set is a collection of non-repeatable and unordered elements, a Bag is a collection that allows repetition and does not impose restrictions on the order of elements, and a List is a specialization of Bag where elements are ordered and repetition is allowed. The other top-level class of the ontology is Item , which serves as an intermediate class to link a Bag with a resource contained within that Bag . Thus, a Bag is linked to an Item through the property item and the Item is linked to a resource via the property itemContent . The fact that the association between a Bag and a resource is done in two steps ( Bag → Item and Item → resource) allows to associate more than once the same resource to a Bag . Moreover, class ListItem is a specialization of Item for representing items of a List . The ordering of items is performed using properties nextItem and previousItem . In the case of Set s, since repetition of elements is not allowed, Set s are linked directly to the resources they contain, through the property element . 1 https://github.com/bdiehu/lop . 2 https://github.com/collections-ontology/collections-ontology/blob/ master/collections.owl . 2.1.2. The sequence ontology design pattern The Sequence ODP 3 is intended to represent sequence schemas. It is characterized by four object properties: precedes , to represent the transitive relation between two individuals where the former in- dividual precedes the latter (e.g. year2021 precedes year2025 ); directlyPrecedes , a subproperty of precedes to represent the intransitive precedence relation (e.g. Monday directlyPrecedes Tuesday ); and their inverse properties follows and directly- Follows . 2.1.3. The set, bag and list ontology design patterns Three relevant ontology design patterns that were extracted from the Collections ontology can be found in the literature: the Set ODP, 4 the Bag ODP 5 and the List ODP 6 (see Fig. 1 7 ). Moreover, some mappings were defined between these ODPs and also with the Sequence ODP. 2.2. Semantic representation of change over time Some approaches exist in the specialized literature that are relevant to the problem of representation of change over time. The N-Ary relation approach [ 15 ] provides a generic solution to represent n-ary relations and could be used to add a temporal context to a fact. Thus, one could have one instance representing the ranking of some com- petition after the first round of fixtures, another one representing that ranking after the second round, and so on. The notion of progression over time could be deduced from the temporal context of each in- stance. In [ 16 ] a 4D or perdurantist view is proposed, in which entities have temporal parts (time slices) that represent them during some time interval. Relations are then established between the time slices, instead between the original entities. The work in [ 17 ] reinterprets this perdurantist/4D view in such a way that entities become time slices that explain the behavior of an entity within a certain temporal interval. Based on this reinterpreted approach, an ODP for representing change over time in OWL is presented in [ 18 ]. Moreover, in [ 19 ], an ODP for representing a series of recurrent situations is presented. Moreover, it could be interesting to define more sophisticated patterns based on simpler collection patterns to allow more complex definitions of collections. Let us define a permutation as an ordered collection of items that does not allow repetitions. Moreover, let us define a list of permutations as an ordered list of permutation s, which could be used, for instance, to keep track of how the order of an original permutation varies along time. Some real use cases of these pattern could be the following: Use case #1: Sports leagues season Throughout a sports league season or championship, a group of teams engage in multiple rounds of fixtures competing against each other. Following each round, the teams’ rankings are adjusted, and the team that secures the topmost position in the rankings after the final round emerges as the champion. However, it could be interesting to collect all the intermediate rankings that were generated during a season/championship, such as in the example in Table 2 , where the rankings of the 2023 Six Nations rugby Championship are recorded. The ranking corresponding to a single round of fixtures could be seen as a permutation of the teams, while the results of the whole championship could be seen as a list of permutations of the ranking. Use case #2: Alternating treatment design Single-Subject Design (SSD) is a research approach that enables the assessment of the effectiveness of interventions on an individual level, offering prompt feedback on the impact of a particular treatment (e.g. Scripting for autism). A subtype of SSD, known as Alternating Treatment Design, involves a two-phase process consisting of a baseline phase with no treatment, followed by an intervention phase where mul- tiple treatments are alternated several times, but not necessarily in the same order. This design is particularly useful for evaluating the effects of various treatments on a single individual over a period of time. For instance, given three treatments A, B and C, ACBCABBACABC and CBAACB are examples of valid alternations because they are composed of blocks [ACB, CAB, BAC, ACB] and [CBA, ABC], respectively, where all three treatments are applied before repeating any of them. sections.heading: C.Q
sections.text: 1.11. Is element x after element y in this permutation? (e.g. was team England after team France in this round of fixtures?) 4.2. Design and implementation One of the requirements that ODPs should meet is to be alignable to other patterns, fostering reuse. Thus, in order to design the ODP Permutation the ODPs presented in Section 2 have been considered. In this process, one could ask the following question: is it a better option to model the main class Permutation as a Set that imposes an order to its elements, or to model it a List that does not allow repetitions? A look at the description of Set in Fig. 1 shows that the first option is not advisable. A Set is linked directly to each resource of the Set by the property hasMember . Imposing the ordering restriction would require to apply the ordering properties (e.g. directlyFollows ) directly in the resources of the Set . If a resource appeared in more than one Permutation , there would be more than one triple with the same resource as subject and the same property and it would not be possible to distinguish the ordering of each Permutation . Thus, we have decided to model a Permutation as a List that does not allow repetitions ( Fig. 2 ). More precisely, the main class Permutation has been defined as a subclass of List . Moreover, it has been stated that Permutation is the target class of a Shapes Con- straint Language (SHACL 8 ) shape named NoRepeatedElemShape 9 : 𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗 ⊑ 𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚝 ∶ 𝙻𝚒𝚜𝚝 𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗 ⊑ ∃ 𝚜𝚑 ∶ 𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚎𝚝𝙲𝚕𝚊𝚜𝚜 − . { 𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚖 ∶ 𝙽𝚘𝚁𝚎𝚙𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎𝚍𝙴𝚕𝚎𝚖𝚂𝚑𝚊𝚙𝚎 } SHACL is a language for validating RDF graphs against a set of conditions that are provided in form of shapes . An extension mecha- nism of SHACL named SHACL-SPARQL also allows the definition of SPARQL-based constraints. The SHACL-SPARQL shape NoRepeatedElemShape that has been defined indicates that there cannot be repeated elements in the instances that belong to the class Permutation . More precisely, it takes the itemContent of each item of the current instance, and checks whether another item with the same itemContent exists among the items that are further in the permutation. If this happens to be true, a Violation will be raised, meaning that the instance of Permutation is not well formed, and issues a message indicating which are the repeated elements. 4.3. Application and evaluation Fig. 3 shows the instantiation of the ODP Permutation to represent the ranking of Round 1 of Table 2 . The main individual Round_1 is a permutation composed of six items be1.1 .. be1.6 , one for each team in the championship. Thus, the content of each item points to a dbpedia resource representing the team (e.g. dbr:Ireland _national_rugby_union_team ). All the competency questions in Section 4.1 can be applied and an- swered. 10 Moreover, in order to check whether Round_1 conforms to the shape NoRepeatedElemShape the TopBraid SHACL 11 validator has been used. The validation report 12 issued by the validator shows that, indeed, Round_1 conforms to the aforementioned shape. Instead, if, for example, instance Round_1 is modified in such a way that be1.5/bag: itemContent points to dbr:France_national _rugby_union _team , thus becoming an invalid instance, the val- idator yields a no-conformant validation report because dbr:France_ national _rugby_union_team is now the bag:itemContent of be1.3 and be1.5 . 5.

sections.heading: C.Q
sections.text: 2.9. In which permutations of the list of permutations is element 𝑥 after element y? (e.g. in which rounds of fixtures was team England after team France during the 2023 Six Nations Championship ?) 5.2. Design and implementation A ListOfPermutations must be a collection that (a) imposes an order to its elements, (b) is composed of elements that belong to the class Permutation , and (c) ensures that each Permutation contains the same elements (in the same or in different order). Thus, the main class ListOfPermutations has been defined as a subclass of a List in which the bag:itemContent of each item belongs to class Permutation . Moreover, it has been stated that ListOfPermutations is the target class of a shape named NoMissingElemShape . 13 A graphical representation of the pattern can be seen in Fig. 4 , while the OWL axioms are presented next: 𝙻𝚒𝚜𝚝𝙾𝚏𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝚜 ⊑ 𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚝 ∶ 𝙻𝚒𝚜𝚝 𝙻𝚒𝚜𝚝𝙾𝚏𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝚜 ⊑ ∀ 𝚋𝚊𝚐 ∶ 𝚑𝚊𝚜𝙸𝚝𝚎𝚖 . (∀ 𝚋𝚊𝚐 ∶ 𝚒𝚝𝚎𝚖𝙲𝚘𝚗𝚝𝚎𝚗𝚝 . 𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚖 ∶ 𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗 ) 𝙻𝚒𝚜𝚝𝙾𝚏𝙿𝚎𝚛𝚖𝚞𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗𝚜 ⊑ ∃ 𝚜𝚑 ∶ 𝚝𝚊𝚛𝚐𝚎𝚝𝙲𝚕𝚊𝚜𝚜 − . { 𝚕𝚘𝚙 ∶ 𝙽𝚘𝙼𝚒𝚜𝚜𝚒𝚗𝚐𝙴𝚕𝚎𝚖𝚂𝚑𝚊𝚙𝚎 } The shape NoMissingElemShape indicates that every permu- tation in a list of permutations must contain the same elements, or in other words, there are not missing elements in any permutation. Thus, a SHACL-SPARQL constraint has been defined which checks whether for every pair of permutations ?perm1 and ?perm2 there exists any element in the permutation ?perm1 that is not contained in the permutation ?perm2 . If this happens to be true, a Violation will be raised, meaning that the instance of ListOfPermutations is not well formed, and issues a message indicating which element is missing in which permutation. One may argue that no indication of specific temporal aspects (e.g. the period of time on which a specific permutation holds) is reflected on the pattern. The main goal of the pattern ListOfPer- mutations is to reflect the changes in the order of the elements rather than to capture temporal aspects. Thus, the notion of time, while inherently related to the concept of change, can be seen as orthogonal to the main purpose of the pattern. Several ontologies exists that allow representing temporal aspects (e.g. OWL-Time 14 ), and their terms could be used when creating instances of the pattern to indicate the temporal context of each permutation (e.g. by using the hasTime object property of the OWL-Time ontology that allows associating a temporal entity with anything). 13 https://github.com/bdiehu/lop/blob/main/listOfPermutations/ implementation/NoMissingElemShape.ttl . 14 https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/ . The main individual sixnations2023 is a list of permu- tations composed of five items bj1 .. bj5 , one for each round in the championship ( Round_1 .. Round_5 ). Each individual Round_x is an instance of Permutation and follows the structure presented for Round_1 in Section 4.3 . All the competency questions in Section 5.1 can be applied and answered. 15 Moreover, the aforementioned validator was used to check whether the list of permutations sixnations2023 conforms to the shape NoMissingElemShape , which it does. When creating an in- valid list of permutations where some element is missing in one or more permutations of the list (e.g. modifying be1.5/bag:itemContent so that it points to an element other than dbr:England_national _rugby_union_team ) a message stating that an element is missing is issued. 6.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: In the definition of both patterns, it has been necessary to resort to SHACL since OWL 2 does not allow modeling at a schema level some of the constraints associated with these patterns. For example, in the case of the pattern Permutation , it is not possible to indicate using OWL 2 that two Item s within the same Permutation cannot 15 https://github.com/bdiehu/lop/tree/main/useCases/SixNations2023/inst antiatedCQs and https://github.com/bdiehu/lop/tree/main/listOfPermutation s/genericCQs . have the same object in the property itemContent . In other words, it cannot be enforced in the definition of a class that two properties or property paths lead to a different object. The same would apply if the properties or property paths had to lead to the same object. In [ 21 ] an example of the latter is found. It can be defined, at a schema level, that an index finger has a middle phalanx and a distal phalanx that is attached to a middle phalanx, but it cannot be enforced that those middle phalanges are indeed the same (or different). Another example can be found in [ 22 ], where the impossibility of defining in OWL 2 a class for representing children whose parents are married to each other is discussed. In that paper, an extension of the description logic SROIQ underlying OWL 2 is presented by introducing a new general constructor, named nominal schema , that would allow to express the aforementioned constraint in the following way: list:nextItem ⊑ furtherItem Trans(furtherItem) list:List ⊓ ∃ bag:hasItem.( ∃ bag:itemContent.{x} ⊓ ∃ furtherItem. ∃ bag:itemContent.{x} ) ≡ NotAPermutation Permutation ≡ list:List ⊓ ¬ NotAPermutation Expression {x} is a nominal schema, which binds for the same known individual in the second axiom, and it can be used to indicate the equality of two itemContent objects. This allows the detection of repeated elements in the collection. However, nominal schemas are theoretical solutions that have not been implemented and are not part of OWL 2, so they could not be used for our purpose. Journal of Web Semantics 85 (2025) 100863 7 I. sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Ontology Design Patterns are used in ontology design in order to address recurring modeling problems. Apart from reusability, they provide other benefits such as consistency and scalability. Several ODPs exist in the literature that allow to represent collections, but none of them is completely appropriate for representing ordered collections without repetition. Therefore, in this paper we have presented a new ODP, Permutation , that allows the representation of collections where elements are ordered and where there cannot be repeated elements. Moreover, on many occasions it is desirable to record how the order of the elements of a permutation changes over time. For this purpose, the ODP ListOfPermutations has been developed. In both cases, it has been necessary to resort to SHACL to define constraints that cannot be expressed in OWL 2.
